title: The Little Catechism of the Pure Note
author: the Choir-Church of the Pure Note, for the instruction of children (a child's copy)
origin: printed for the parishes of the Resonant Reach
summary: The questions and answers every child of the Reach learns before confirmation, in a copy that once belonged to a Greenroot girl.
text: THE LITTLE CATECHISM OF THE PURE NOTE. For the instruction of children before their confirmation in the Light. Set forth under the seal of His Resonance the High Patriarch, to be learned by heart, said in the Narrow, and never sung except in the Church's keeping.

To the teacher. Let the child give each answer in one breath and on one pitch. If the voice rises or falls within an answer, let the child say it again until it does not. This is not unkindness. It is the first lesson.
OF THE LIGHT
Q. Who made the world?  A. The Architects, who came out of the Light and pinned the world to eight Spires, so that it would not fall.
Q. Why does the apple grow, and the fire warm, and the stone fall?  A. Because the Spires are singing, each its own law, and none of them has ever stopped.
Q. Do the Spires grow tired?  A. No. What is holy does not tire.
Q. Who keeps the Spires?  A. The Iron Synod, which the Light appointed. One Note. One Law. One Hand.
Q. What is Aether-Glass?  A. The Light's generous surplus, given so that we may be warm and fed and carried. It would be ungrateful to leave it in the ground.
OF HOLINESS
Q. What is holiness?  A. One note, held without end.
Q. What is sin?  A. The second note.
Q. Is the second note wicked?  A. It is a crack. Through a crack the whole jar empties.
Q. What is the Pure Note?  A. Five hundred and twenty-eight, the Light's own pitch, which the choirs hold for us so that we need not.
Q. Why did the world go flat?  A. Because in the Screaming Year a dissonance was raised at the Dawning, and the Light was wounded, and every note in the world went a little wrong.
Q. Will it be mended?  A. When every voice holds one note, the Light will be whole.
OF THE NARROW
Q. Why must I speak low?  A. Because the hounds come to noise, and most noise is the second note.
Q. Why must I not be silent?  A. Because a silent child is a sullen child, and the hush-lamp is there to remind me.
Q. What is the Hush?  A. A thing we do not speak of in the Church, because the Pure Note is never silent.
Q. May I sing?  A. Not alone, and not in the open, and not in two parts. Only in the Church's keeping, where the Pure Flame goes before the choir.
Q. Why do the hounds not come to the choir?  A. Because the Flame goes before it, and they will not cross the Flame. This shows that they know what is holy.
OF THE KEPT
Q. Who are the Consecrated?  A. Those in whom the Light has set its glass, so that they may be kept.
Q. Who is our Queen?  A. Maelis, whom the Light has kept long past her dying, and whose hand does not shake.
Q. Is she afraid?  A. The kept are never afraid.
Q. What is the highest thing a voice may do?  A. Hold the Pure Note for the Light for as long as it is asked, and not let it waver.
Q. And if it hurts?  A. Then I offer the hurt, and hold.
OF THE PURE FLAME
Q. What shall I do if I hear the second note in my own mouth?  A. Close my mouth, and tell my mother, and tell the priest.
Q. What shall I do if I hear the second note in my mother's mouth?  A. Love her, and tell the priest.
Q. What is done with the second note?  A. Where it has taken root, it is given to the Pure Flame, which is the only song.
Q. Is the Flame cruel?  A. The Flame is mercy. It does not hurt what is pure.

A PRAYER AT THE HUSH-LAMP, to be said low, at bedtime: Light, keep me true. Keep my mouth to one note. Keep my house from the second note, and my street from the hounds, and if I wake in the dark, let the lamp be whistling.
Inside the back board, in pencil, in a child's round hand:
Dilly Teale her book. Greenroot. Lernt to the end.
Below it, in the same hand and the same pencil, a question of her own, set out properly with a Q and an A, the way she had been taught:
Q. Why has the lamp stopped whistling.
A.
She has left the rest of the line for the answer.
notes: Canon: the catechism's two questions on holiness and sin (Series Bible Part III; Book One prologue epigraph); Church teaching that the Architects pinned the world to eight Spires, the Synod is steward and Aether-Glass is the Light's generous surplus (Series Bible Part III, 'What everyone believes'); 'One Note. One Law. One Hand.' (Part VII); the glassed called Consecrated, Queen Maelis's famously steady signature, the Flambeaux's glass-fire that the Cacophony will not cross (Part VII); the Pure Note 528 (Part VI); 'Where the second note has taken root, let the Pure Flame be the only song' (Book One Ch7 epigraph, Warrant of Purification); the Church's official cause of the Fracture as 'a dissonance from the gantry' (Book One, the Inquisitorial report, manuscript l.5722); 'the World Went Flat' and the Screaming Year (Series Bible Part IV, V); hush-lamps, the Narrow (Part IV). Greenroot fell silent in 417 and its last register ends with the hush-lamp's reed as the only sound left (js/parish.js REGISTER_PAGES); the pencil note is written to sit beside that without stating anything. The Hush is not described. 'Light, keep me true' adapts the Heights greeting (Vol II Realm II dialect). [PROPOSED]: the Little Catechism as a printed book and its 416 printing; all questions beyond the canon pair; the instruction to answer on one pitch; Dilly Teale, a Greenroot child, and her copy. Library: the Greenroot chapel, or found.

title: The Only Song: A Sermon to the Flambeaux Going Out
author: Lucan Ostrel, Flambeau-Preceptor
origin: the Basilica of the Pure Note; printed so that every Flambeau might carry a copy
summary: The sermon preached to new Flambeaux on the eve of their going out to the provinces, on why the Church alone sings aloud, and why it burns.
text: Preached to the Flambeaux of the year's going-out, on the eve of their dispersal to the provinces, in the Basilica of the Pure Note, and printed so that each of them might carry it. Where the second note has taken root, let the Pure Flame be the only song.
Brothers. Sisters. Tomorrow you go out, and tonight I will tell you what you are going into, because nobody told me.

You are going into the whispering country. You will come to towns where nobody has raised a voice in six years. They have hedges where their walls were and thorn where their gates were, and in every room a lamp with a reed in it that whistles all night so that the house is never quite silent. They will speak to you in what they call the Narrow, the strip of voice they have left between too loud and too still, and they will tell you it is wisdom. They teach it to their children as a skipping rhyme. Listen to the rhyme. Then ask yourself what kind of province teaches its children to skip to their own fear.

I do not despise them. Hear that before anything else. I was born in a valley like those valleys, and my mother hummed me into the world through a clay jar. They are not wicked. They are frightened, and fear has a pitch, and it is never the true one.

Now hear what you are. You are the only people in Aethelgard who walk in the open, singing. The hounds come to every voice in the world but yours. They will pace the tree-line beside your procession. You will see them, a shaking in the air like heat over a summer road, keeping step with you, and they will not come in. Ask yourselves why. It is not because you are brave. I have known Flambeaux who were not brave. It is the Flame. The Light gave us glass-fire, white and gold, out of its own surplus, and nothing hungry will cross it. That is not a weapon. It is a testimony. The Light has drawn a line on the ground around the one note and written: here, nothing comes.
So you will sing aloud, and they will stare at you from behind their hands. Let them stare. You are the thing they have forgotten is possible: a voice raised, and alive afterwards.

You will be asked about the burning. You will be asked by the people in the hedges, and by magistrates who cannot read our warrants, and at last by yourselves, in the third hour of the night, which is the hour the question comes. I will answer it now, so that you have the answer in your mouth when you need it.

The second note is not a wickedness of the heart. I have given women to the Flame who were kinder than I am, and I knew it at the time. The second note is a crack. In a jar a crack is a small thing. You can hold the jar to the window and hardly see it, and the jar empties through it all the same.

Consider a town in the whispering country. Four hundred souls, holding their breath. In one house a woman hums her child to sleep at an open window, in two parts, because her grandmother did and it is a pretty thing. You know what comes to it. And when it comes, it does not come only to her window. A pack that has found one door walks the whole street. One lullaby. A hundred doors.

Consider the burl-sick: the second note taken root in the flesh. A woman grown into her chair. A child with bark at the wrist. The Grafters cut, and the root comes back, and they cut again, and it comes back again, because you cannot cut a note out of a body. The flesh is singing the wrong song and will go on singing it, and every night it sings, the hounds sit a little closer to the hedge.

You will be told that this is cruelty. I tell you it is arithmetic, and the Light did the sum before we were born. The Flame does not hurt what is pure. What it takes, it was always going to take. You choose only whether it takes one house or the street.

Now the hardest thing, and then I will let you sleep. When you stand at the warrant's hour with the stave lifted, do not weep. Weep afterwards. I do. Weep in your cell, into your sleeve, at the foot of the Spire if you are ever let near it. Not at the hour. A flame held in a shaking hand is a flame that wavers, and a wavering flame is a second note, and the hounds know the difference better than you do.

In some of those towns there will be a Cantor. There are fewer every year. She will be the kindest person you meet, and she will look at you as if you were the thing at the tree-line. Be gentle with her. She has spent her life singing second notes to apple trees and calling it a craft, and she does not know what she has been doing. Most of them do not. That is not their sin. It is ours, for leaving them so long without the Light.

Go out singing. Let them hear you coming a mile off, as they have not heard anything coming in six years, and let them hate you for it from behind their thorn. They will be alive to hate you. That is the whole of our ministry, and it is enough.
And when you come to the gate of a whispering town, do not lower your voice. Nothing that holds the one note has ever needed to.
notes: Canon: the Flambeaux, glass-fire fed on amber Aether-Glass which the Cacophony will not cross, the Church alone singing aloud in the open (Series Bible Part VII, Choir-Church); the Warrant of Purification's line used as the text (Book One Ch7 epigraph); hounds pacing the tree-line beside the procession, 'a jitter in the air ... like heat above a summer road' (Book One Ch7, manuscript l.2271); the burl-sick, roots and Grafters (Part VI, the Reach); hymns bring hounds (Part IV, the World Went Flat); births hummed through clay jars, hedges, hush-lamps, the skipping rhyme (Part IV, Part VI); 'fear has a pitch' (Vol II Bestiary, universal rules); Cantors' craft as the second note the Church calls sin (Part III, the lost curriculum); hours of the night counted from dark (Vol VII §5). 'Six years' fits 418. [PROPOSED]: Lucan Ostrel, Flambeau-Preceptor, and the office of Preceptor; the annual going-out of Flambeaux from the Basilica of the Pure Note (the Basilica is canon, Vol VI §3.3) and the printed sermon. A copy plausibly travels with the Inquisitor's procession to Oakhaven's Chapel of the Pure Note. Library: the Oakhaven chapel or vestry; could also be found in the Conservatory, confiscated.

title: Already Quiet: A Word for Those Who Are Tired
author: a brother of the Quiet Faith, unsigned (he has given back his name)
origin: the Deep Woods, copied out by hand
summary: A hand-copied tract of the Tongueless, written for people worn out by the Narrow, inviting them into the woods.
text: I am writing this because I cannot say it. That is the first thing to understand about us, and it is the last. Read it slowly. Read it inside your head. You need not move your lips. You have moved your lips enough.

You are tired. I know you are tired, because I was. You have lived seven years in the Narrow. You have weighed every word you spoke against two deaths, the one that comes to loud things and the one that comes to still things, and you have spoken between them, low, all day, every day, so carefully that you no longer know what your own voice sounds like when it is not afraid. There is a lamp in your room that whistles all night so that your house is never silent, and you have not slept a night through since it was lit. You hum at crossings. You hum your children into the world through jars. You bind the jaws of your dead so that they cannot ring.

Who made the rhyme? Too loud brings the hounds, too still brings the Hush. Somebody frightened made it, and you have skipped to it ever since. I ask you to look at its two halves side by side, the way you would look at two men offering you work.

The hounds. You know what they do. Everyone in the siphoned country has heard a neighbour's voice taken at the hedge, and heard it come back afterwards out of the dark, asking for his wife. That is what loudness brings. It is what the Church brings, walking singing down your roads behind its fire, and what the Synod brings with its drills, and what your Cantors bring when they love somebody too much to keep quiet.

Now the other half. Tell me what the Quiet has done to you. Not what you were told. What you saw. You saw a house go still. You saw a kettle boil that nobody could hear. You saw a man sit down by the Flume with his hands open in his lap. Think of his face. Was it afraid? Did he scream? Has anyone, in the whole of the siphoned country, ever once heard one of them scream?

No. Nobody screams. Every one of us who has watched has said the same thing afterwards, in the same words, without being taught them: it does not hurt. They look relieved. They look like a man setting down a load at the end of a long day's carrying.
And that is the thing you were taught to be afraid of, by a rhyme, by a lamp, and by a priest.

This is what we do, and why. We cut out our own tongues, so that we cannot answer. The voices at the hedge call you by your name, in the voices of the people you loved, and the only safety the world has ever offered you against them is the rule that you must not answer. We have made it so that we cannot. No hound has ever learned my voice. None ever will. There is nothing left in me to hunt. And when the Quiet comes, as it comes to everything at last, it will find me already quiet, already its own, and it will not need to take anything from me at all. I will go with it the way you go with someone who has come to walk you home.
We do not ask you to cut. We ask you to stop being afraid of the wrong thing.

Some of you have heard what we do with the children who sing. I will tell it plainly, because you have heard it told unkindly. There are children who will not keep the Narrow. They sing; they cannot help it; it is in them the way the second note was in the old orchard-singers. In a town such a child brings the hounds to every door, and then the Church comes and burns the house for it. We burn nobody. We take the singing child out at evening, past the last lamp, into the trees, and we leave her there singing, as a gift, and we go back to our fires and we do not listen. In the morning the singing has stopped. There is no mark on the moss. Nothing has been torn. Nothing is ever torn. That is how we know she was received kindly.

Our Abbess has letters. They come a long way, sealed in plain grey with no device on the seal, in a hand that has stopped wasting ink, and a brother who kept his tongue for that purpose alone reads them to us by the fire. The one who writes them has listened longer than any of us. He writes that everything which sings is tired, all of it, everywhere, and has been tired for longer than anyone can count, and wants only to be allowed to put the weight down. He writes that the Quiet is not a death but a rest. We believed it before he wrote. Still, it was a comfort to learn that someone so far away, and so learned, had come to the same place by another road.

If you are tired, come into the woods. Not tonight. Tonight you are afraid, and fear has a pitch, and you would be heard. Come when you are tired enough that it has stopped mattering to you what hears you. You will know the night. Leave your lamp unlit behind you. Walk until the reed in the last window has faded out at your back, and keep walking, and when you can no longer hear your own feet, you will know that you are among friends.

I gave back my name when I gave back my tongue. I kept my hand only so long as it took to copy this out forty times, which is the number the Abbess asked of me. This is the fortieth. When it is finished I will put down the pen, and I will not pick anything up again.
notes: Canon: the Tongueless, the Quiet Faith, the Merciful Quiet, tongues cut to be 'already quiet', children who sing left in the woods as hush-gifts, the Abbess leading in hand-cant, and 'Vaelen's agents feed them scripture' (Series Bible Part VII, The Tongueless); the mimic rule and the voices at the Hedge (Part IV; Book One Ch6, Ch11); the Hush's rules: nobody screams, it is always kind, 'it does not hurt', aftermath only (Vol IV §1.3, §1.7, §1.8); Greenroot's kettle that boiled unheard (js/parish.js register); 'fear has a pitch' (Vol II Bestiary). The grey seal with no device and 'a hand that has stopped wasting ink' echo Vaelen's letter (Vol VI §5, The Visit) as a hint only; the writer is never named and nothing about the Choristers is stated. Harm to a child is present but not rendered. The Hush is never described: only a still house, a kettle, a face. Shelve after the Greening only (Phase 13 lore note: no Quiet Faith named in any line before it). [PROPOSED]: the tract and its forty hand copies; a brother who keeps his tongue to read the letters aloud; the grey-sealed letters to the Abbess (the Abbess is not named here). Library: the Deep Woods camp, or found on a Tongueless brother.

title: Off the Slate: Sayings of the Cantor-Master
author: Ilse Brennan, Cantor-Master of Reedside; copied before the rag by her pupil Hazel Thrup
summary: The sayings of a voiceless old teacher of Cantors, copied off her slate by a pupil before they could be wiped away.
text: Mistress Brennan lost her voice in the throat-fever of 408, after nine nights of singing the sick. She has taught by slate ever since, and by her hands, and by her breath, and at the end of every lesson she wipes the slate with a wet rag, because, she says, a slate is for saying things and not for keeping them. Some of us began copying them before the rag. She knows. She has never stopped us, which is how we know she does not mind, and she has never once said so, which is how we know she is a Cantor.
They are set down here the way the orchard sets things down: by what was growing.
WHEN THE GROUND IS SOFT
Four counts in. A long fall out. You will do this ten thousand times before you are any use to anybody, and ten thousand more after.
A Cantor's instrument is the breath. The voice is only the most common way of spending it.
Trees hear breath before voice. So do the dying. So, if you are honest, do you.
Do not be careful. Be exact. Careful is a fear in an apron. Exact is a craft.
WHEN THE REEDS COME UP

The reeds came up every spring of my life until the Screaming Year, and then they turned to glass in an hour and blew away. Hang the First Reeds over the doors anyway. A reed that does not sound is still a reed. It is still somebody's child's.
The tending note is not yours. You are carrying it for someone. Carry it the way you carry a bowl that is too full: slowly, looking at the bowl and not at your feet.
Ask with the hand. Lay it flat on the bark. Be still. A tree will answer a still hand before it answers a clever one, and so will a frightened man.
MIDSUMMER

In the Chapel, one note. In the orchard, as many as the tree asks for. Do not tell the Chapel about the orchard. (She wiped this one before any of us had finished copying it. I have put it together from three of us.)

The Narrow is not a cage. It is a reed. Too much breath and it shrieks; too little and it is dead. Every Cantor in the Reach has played that reed all her life. Now everyone has to, and they are angry that it is hard. Be kind to them. It is hard.
Sing the birth through the jar. The jar is not there to keep the sound in. It is there to make the sound small enough to hold.
A child who will not cry is a door left open. Hum at it until it is cross with you. Cross is alive.
Too loud is a good problem. Too quiet is a good problem. Not caring which is the only bad one.
HARVEST
Never sing to a thing you will not stay with.
The felling-song is not a goodbye. It tells the sap it may go down now. You learn it last, at sixteen, and I hope you will need it seldom. You will not need it seldom.
Hum while they bind the jaw and lay the stone on the tongue. It is the last thing they will hear, and it ought to be kind, and it ought to be low.

Written on the morning we heard about the orchard-cantor, in the spring of 417: Tobin Ashgrove went above the Narrow for a fevered child, and the child lived. Do not make him a lesson. He would hate it. Make him a reason. (Most of us cried. She let us. Then she cleaned the slate, and we did the breath.)
THE COLD MONTHS

On the Longest Night, hum into the hollow of the oldest tree in the orchard. My teacher did not know why. Her teacher did not know why. Do it anyway, and do it well, as though somebody were listening who had waited all year for you.

You will lose your voice one day. Every Cantor does, to the fever or the years or the one night when it was needed all at once. When it goes, you will find out what you were really using. I am still finding out.

Somebody asked her once, in my second year, whether she missed singing. She wrote: I have not stopped. Then she breathed the tending note at the window, four in and the long fall out, and the frost on the inside of the glass went off it in a ring the size of a hand.
THIS YEAR

The Last Sheaf has been forbidden. The Church has set its Rite for the same week, and the town has been told to put the harvest off. On the morning the notice went up, Mistress wrote one line on her slate and turned it to face the window, towards the north field, where the last stand is still uncut. She did not wipe it. It is there as I write this. I have copied it so that it is kept somewhere, though she would say that is not what slates are for.
CUT IT ANYWAY. QUIETLY. THINGS ARE ALLOWED TO END.
notes: Canon: Ilse Brennan, Cantor-Master of the Reedside Conservatory for forty years, Lyra's teacher, voice lost in 408 after nine nights singing in the throat-fever, teaches by slate, hands and breath; her line 'A Cantor's instrument is the breath...' (Vol V §4, Ilse Brennan); the tending breath, 'trees hear breath before voice', asking with the hand, the felling-song learned at sixteen, stone on the tongue (Vol V §4, Reach Customs, Felling-Song); humming into the hollow of the oldest orchard tree on the Longest Night as a remnant custom, here unexplained (Vol V §4, the Cantors' Secret; the old stair is kept sealed for Book Four per Release Readiness item 7); wind-reeds turned to sugar-glass in the Cascade, births through clay jars, a silent child as a door left open (Series Bible Part IV, Part VI); First Reeds over doors (Vol I §4.3); Tobin Ashgrove taken in 417 raising his voice for a fevered child (Part VIII); the Reach dates by what is growing (Vol VII §8); the Last Sheaf forbidden in 419 because of the Rite, the uncut stand in the north field (Vol VII (b) §2); 'too loud ... a good problem' sits with Lyra's line to the child in the Deep Woods (js/data.js NPCS.wren_dw) without claiming Lyra quoted it. No new facts about Lyra. [PROPOSED]: Hazel Thrup, a pupil; the slate-and-rag habit and the copying; every saying not quoted above; the frost-ring anecdote. Library: the Conservatory in Oakhaven, which Ilse Brennan keeps; a second copy could sit in Lyra's house.

title: A Digest of the Standing Law, for Magistrates of the Resonant Reach
author: the Arbiterium of the Iron Synod; with marginal notes by Septimus Fallow, clerk to the bench at Oakhaven
origin: the Organum; the margins written at the Oakhaven watch-house
summary: The Synod's handbook of law for Reach magistrates, and the increasingly personal notes of the clerk who has had to apply it in a town behind a hedge.
text: A DIGEST OF THE STANDING LAW OF THE IRON SYNOD, abridged for the use of Governors, Reeves and Magistrates in the Resonant Reach. Issued under the Scales by the Arbiterium, at the Organum. Third issue, 414. One Note. One Law. One Hand.

On the flyleaf, in a small brown hand: Property of the bench, Oakhaven watch-house. Annotated by S. Fallow, clerk, who has read it more often than the men who wrote it. The notes are mine and the law is theirs. I have tried to keep the two apart and have not always managed.

PREFACE. The magistrate is not required to understand the law. He is required to apply it. Where an article appears to him to conflict with local custom, the article prevails, and the custom is to be reported.
Clerk's note: I have reported the custom of the Narrow eleven times. I have had no reply. I take it the custom prevails until somebody in the Organum can be found who has heard of it.

ARTICLE THE FIRST. Of the posting of writs. A writ of the Arbiterium has force from the hour of its posting at the gate of the place named. Its statutory period runs from the posting, and not from any reading.
Note: Oakhaven's gate is now a gap in a hedge of thorn and packed wool three men deep. I have posted the last four writs on the thorn. The thorn has kept them. I cannot get the third one back out.
ARTICLE THE SECOND. Of reading aloud. No writ touching a named person is served until it has been read aloud, in a clear and carrying voice, before witnesses.

Note: Clear and carrying. I have read a writ in a clear and carrying voice twice in my life, in '13 and in '14, and both times we lost somebody at the gate that night. I now read them to old Harrow in the gatehouse, in the Narrow, with my mouth an inch from his ear, and he witnesses with his thumb. Whether Oakhaven has been lawfully served with anything since '15 is a question I have decided not to put to the Arbiterium.

ARTICLE THE THIRD. Of standing writs. A writ under black ribbon is a standing writ. It shall be carried by hand to the person named and put into his hand, and its bearer shall not stop, nor be stopped, until it is delivered.
Note: The one article in this book that the Reach keeps without being told. Nobody stops for anything here any more.

ARTICLE THE FOURTH. Of attainder. Persons declared Dissonant under the standing form forfeit their goods; their testimony is void in any court of the Synod; their names are struck. Provided always that grace is offered to each, once.

Note: Once. In '16 I wrote to the Arbiterium to ask what follows if grace is refused and afterwards, on reflection, wanted. The answer came in eleven weeks. It quoted the form back to me: a man who refuses grace has chosen what follows. I had read the form. That was why I asked. (The blots on this page are the pen's, which catches.)

ARTICLE THE FIFTH. Of Symmetry. That law may never wound one without wounding the other, an Arbiter and his heir shall be bound in Symmetry, wound for wound, and neither shall outlive the other by an hour. (Edict of 389.) The magistrate need take no notice of this article, which touches the Arbiters alone.
Note: The only article in the book that binds the men who wrote it. It is also the only one with no penalty in it. I have thought about that more than a clerk should.
ARTICLE THE SIXTH. Of requisition. All bells, chimes and resonant metal within the province are requisitioned to the public works under the Consortium's warrant. A receipt shall be given.

Note: Ours went in '17, every one, the chapel's first. I have the receipt. It is the best-made piece of paper in Oakhaven. It says the bells have gone to the public works. It does not say what part of a work a bell becomes.
ARTICLE THE SEVENTH. Of assembly. No assembly of more than twelve persons shall be held for the purpose of song, save in the Church's keeping.
Note: We have not put twelve people together to sing since the Screaming Year, Synod or no Synod. The hounds drafted this one before the Arbiterium did.

ARTICLE THE EIGHTH. Of the Church. A warrant of purification under the seal of the High Patriarch is a matter for the Church and is not cognisable by a magistrate. No appeal lies from it to any bench. The Arbiterium alone may stay it.

Note: Not cognisable: that is, I may not know of it. It was read in the square on Dawnday, aloud, by a herald whose voice went up over the roofs as if he had never been told there was any other way to speak. Eighty-four souls in the Hollow; nineteen of them children. I have the census. I looked up the remedy. There is one. It is a stay from the Arbiterium, to be asked for in writing, at the Organum. The fire is on Hearthday.

ARTICLE THE NINTH. Of registration. Persons removing from the province under transit warrant shall present themselves to the Office of the Catalogue for registration at the first relief station. Registration is a condition of transit and may not be declined.

Note: Nobody has been given transit out of Oakhaven since the hedge went up, so this article has never been tried here. The Office has sent us the forms all the same. Four hundred of them, already numbered.

ARTICLE THE TENTH. Of persons under the mark. A person whom a Surgeon-Grafter has marked as past cutting shall be struck from the roll of the bench and of the census, and his testimony shall be received only upon the affidavit of a sound witness.

Note: Marked, Massday. Master Rooke did it himself, at my own table, and was gentle about it, and told me the mark means past cutting and nothing else, which I believe of him; and I have also read the warrant. I am entering it here because it is a fact, and the bench ought to have it, and a clerk enters things. My hand is not what it was. The nails want paring twice a day now, and by noon the ink is under them again. My wife has signed below as my sound witness, so that this note will be good in law.
Below, in a different and steadier hand: Witnessed. M. Fallow. He was a good clerk. He is a good clerk.
notes: Canon: the Arbiterium, writs posted at the gate with the statutory period running from the posting (Vol VI §5, Justiciary practice); a writ must be read aloud and witnessed (Book One Ch24, manuscript l.6190); a black-ribbon Arbiterium writ is a standing writ that must be delivered (Book One Ch21, l.5630); the standing form of Attainder and Grace, quoted (Book One Ch24 epigraph, l.6162); the Edict of Symmetry, 389, quoted (Vol VI §5); 'One Note. One Law. One Hand.' (Series Bible Part VII); bells taken for bore-teeth (Part VI, the Reach); the Hedge of thorn and packed wool, three men deep (Part VI; Phase 20-21 Rulings); old Harrow the gate-warden (Part VIII); the Warrant of Purification read aloud in the square on Dawnday, the Hollow to burn on Hearthday, 84 souls and 19 children (Book One Ch7, l.2303-2311, l.2453); Rooke's green sap-mark meaning past cutting and the warrant naming the marked houses (Book One Ch3, l.1067-1071); registration as a condition of transit (Book One Ch18, l.4944); the Arbiterium's power to stay the Church's claim (Book One Ch24). Nothing is said of what registration leads to. [PROPOSED]: this digest and its 414 issue; Articles Seven, Nine and Ten as worded, including the striking of marked persons from the census; Septimus Fallow, clerk to the Oakhaven bench, and his wife M. Fallow; his letter of '16; the four hundred numbered forms. Library: the Oakhaven watch-house; could also be found or sold.

title: The Undertow, Extraordinary Number: To the Reach, Which Cannot Shout
author: the Undertow, Broadsheet Row, Port Cantabile (unsigned)
origin: Broadsheet Row, Port Cantabile; carried up the river through Stillwater Landing
summary: A seditious Cantabile broadsheet printed small to fold small, written for the whispering towns of the Reach and smuggled in by the river.
text: THE UNDERTOW. Broadsheet Row, Port Cantabile. Extraordinary Number, printed small to fold small. Price one penny to the lockman at Stillwater, who will charge you two. Not for sale in the Reach, where nothing is for sale that the works store does not sell.
TO THE REACH, WHICH CANNOT SHOUT, FROM A STREET THAT CANNOT STOP.
Friends up the river. We are told you read in a whisper now. Good. Whisper this.

You were hungry after the Screaming Year, and a company came up your road with forty wagons of grain and a paper. You ate the grain. Nobody blames you. We would have eaten it. But you might ask, the next time you stand at the works store paying for bread with the green-and-black paper they pay your sons in, who owns the store, and who owns the paper, and who owns the bread, and whether there is anything left in Oakhaven that a man is paid in and can spend anywhere else.

They took your bells. Every bell in the Reach, for 'the public works'. Ask what a bell is for at the bottom of a bore. We asked an engineer. He drank what we bought him and said 'teeth', and would say no more, and was gone before the second glass.

They gave you a Hedge instead. Thorn and wool, three men deep, to swallow your sounds. You planted it yourselves, by hand, in a few days and nights, and we hear it was the bravest piece of work done in that province in a hundred years. Now ask which side of it the works are on, and which side of it you are.

THE BELL-HELMS. There is a garrison of Carillon Legionnaires at your quarry gate. Stand close to one, if you can bear to, and listen. Every soldier who has served beside them has heard it: somebody is murmuring inside the helm. We do not say whose voice. We do not know. We say only that crates come up this coast marked 'components', very carefully packed, and go inland by air; and that a man who loaded them for two seasons at Driftwood Cay told us in the Lantern Yard that they talk in their sleep. Then he stopped coming to the Lantern Yard. His wife does not know where he is either.

WHISPER-GROVE. Three years ago a city of seventy-four thousand forgot itself in a night, and the Synod's Gazette called it a regrettable resonance event and put a cordon round it. Our neighbour on the Row, whom we do not like and who does not like us, printed what his men saw inside the cordon. We have checked it. He was right. We say so through our teeth.

THE CHURCH. Its processions are out on the roads this year under glass-fire, with warrants in boxes. They sing the whole way, aloud, in daylight, and the hounds pace them along the tree-line and do not come in. You will want very badly to believe that this means something. It means that they have the one fire the hounds will not cross, and they have never once offered to share it with you.

WHAT WE ASK. Nothing. We are a newspaper. The Harbour lets the Row print because the Row has never asked anybody to do anything, and we are not fools enough to start. We only say that we hear things go missing in the Reach: a cart, a carter, a whole parish on the Flume road where nobody answers letters now. Write to us. The lockman at Stillwater will carry a letter down the river for a penny. He will read it first and sell what is in it to five other people, so write it plain, and write it as if all five were reading, because they are.

HOW TO KEEP THIS. Do not burn it. Smoke carries, and the Flambeaux have noses. Do not read it aloud: they say the bell-helms keep everything they hear and can be made to say it all back. Fold it in eight and put it in a hymnal in your chapel, at the page for the Pure Note, where nobody ever needs to look. Somebody will find it. That is how it found you.

A WORD FROM THE ROW. Our compositor of the last number is not with us. He was careful and he was quick, and he set this paper for nine years without a literal in it. We have set this one ourselves, and you will find the mistakes. Leave them. They are how you know it was us.
notes: Canon: Broadsheet Row, the only free press on the continent, four papers, all libellous, one occasionally correct (Vol II Realm VI; Vol I §III.6); Cantabile broadsheets reaching the Reach through Stillwater Landing, whose lockkeeper sells the same news to six parties (Vol II Realm I; Phase 16 text, landing and lockkeeper lines; Review - The Moor serial, ruling 11); a Cantabile broadsheet published the Whisper-Grove story (Vol I §III.6; Vol II); 74,000 Unnamed in 416 (Series Bible Part V); the grain wagons (Book One Ch2); green-and-black scrip (Book One Ch4); bells taken for bore-teeth and the Hedge planted by the town (Part VI; Phase 20-21 Rulings); Legionnaires murmuring inside the helm (Part VII), told here as rumour only, with no claim about what they are; crates of 'components' carried by air (Book One Ch4, Ch8; Phase 6 'Cantabile Candour' counterpoint); glass-fire processions and hounds pacing the tree-line (Book One Ch7); Legion cores keeping what they hear, given as 'they say' (Series Bible Part IV, Unnaming); Driftwood Cay, the Lantern Yard (Vol II; Part X-B); the Synod Gazette (Phase 6 UI strings); Greenroot's silence in 417 (js/parish.js), not named. The rival who printed Whisper-Grove is left unnamed because the Pell name is a trap. [PROPOSED]: the Undertow as one of the Row's four papers; this Extraordinary Number; the Gazette's phrase 'regrettable resonance event'; the missing loader and the missing compositor; the Harbour tolerating the Row. Library: the Bonded Store at Stillwater Landing, or found folded in a chapel hymnal.

title: The Rule of the House: Of the Keeping of Names
author: the Silent Veil; copied fair by the scribe styled Umber
year: c. 290 SR (the Rule itself is far older)
origin: the House of the Silent Veil, in the Spectral Woods
summary: The Veil's rule for its scribes: why they keep names, why they never lift a hand, and what they give up to do it.
text: THE RULE OF THE HOUSE. Of the keeping of names, and why. To be read to every scribe on the evening before she takes the pen, and again on any evening she asks for it.
Over the door of the House it is cut in our notation: What is written is not lost. Read it as a promise and you will be disappointed. Read it as a duty and you will be a scribe.
The House keeps three rules. Write what happened. Write who it happened to. Do not comfort yourself in the margin. Everything else in this book is only those three, explained to someone tired.

OF THE FIRST RULE. Write what happened: not what was meant to happen, nor what the powers say afterwards happened, nor what you would have liked. Every kingdom is rewritten by whoever outlives it, and the rewriting begins within the year. The House is the one place in the world where the first account is kept against the second. We have outlived eight crowns doing this. We expect to outlive the Synod, which is young.

OF THE SECOND RULE. Write who it happened to. The novice thinks she understands this rule, and does not. The powers will always write that a town was lost. We write the town's names: all of them, in the order we can learn them, with the age and the trade, and the last thing said, if anyone heard it. A loss without names is weather. A loss with names is a crime, or a grief, or both, and it can be answered.

WHY THE NAME. Because the name is the last thing that belongs to a person when everything else has gone to the ground or the fire or the powers. Because the world forgets on a curve, steep at first and then slow, and every name slides down that curve, and the House stands at the bottom of it with a cup. Because a name kept is a door left on the latch. We do not know who will come through it. We keep it on the latch.

A name written in the House is held. It is not to be spent, nor lent, nor sold, nor set to any work, nor counted towards any sum but the sum of the dead. A scribe who uses a name for anything but its keeping has stopped being a scribe and become a kind of merchant, and the House has a word for that which it does not write down.

OF THE THIRD RULE. Do not comfort yourself in the margin. You will want to. You will stand in a burning town with your desk on your knees and write the names of the people going past you into the fire, and you will want to write beside them that you were sorry, that you wept, that nothing could be done. Do not. The margin is not yours. Every word of comfort you write there is a word taken from them.

OF THE STILL HAND. You will ask, as every novice asks: why do we only write? Why do we not carry water? Hear the answer the House has given for a thousand years, and then decide whether you can bear it. A scribe who carries water is one more pair of hands in the burning town, and burns with it, and then nobody writes. The powers do not fear our hands. They fear the record. A scribe who takes a side is a witness for that side, and a witness for a side can be answered. A scribe who takes none cannot. So we stand still and write, and are hated by everyone in the town, and are not answered. That is the price of the record. The scribe pays it, and she does not get to stop paying it by feeling bad. If you cannot bear it, lay down the pen tonight. There is no shame in that. There is only no place for you here.

OF THE SCRIBE'S OWN NAME. On the evening you take the pen, you give your name into the House. It is written once, in the Prior's hand, and sealed, and laid in the cabinet in the scriptorium, and kept against the day you lay the pen down, when it is given back to you at the door. Until then you are styled by a colour or a creature, as every scribe before you was. This is not unkindness. A scribe who carries her own name into a burning town will write it into every page. Leave it here. It will be safe. Nothing in the House is ever lost.

OF MEMORYDAY. On Memoryday, at dusk, the duty-scribe stands in the lower hall with a lamp and reads one page of the dead aloud, unhurried, in the voice for entries, so that they are heard. Nobody has been able to tell the House why this was begun. The page is read all the same, every eighth day, and no book we hold records a Memoryday it was missed.
Here the Rule ends. Beneath it, in a smaller hand and a browner ink:

Copied fair by the scribe styled Umber, in the House, in the winter the Synod's surveyors came. They measured every room and wrote a name for the House on their plan which is not its name, and asked the Prior a great many questions about the cabinet, very politely. I have kept the third rule in every margin of my life but this one. We cleaned the desks with vinegar today for the end of the month, and the scriptorium is very cold, and I am afraid.
Across the foot of the page, in red, a later stamp:
RECEIVED INTO THE OFFICE OF THE CATALOGUE, WITH THE HOUSE AND ITS CONTENTS. RETAINED AGAINST NEED.
notes: Canon: the Silent Veil as an independent order of archivists absorbed c. 300 SR as the Office of the Catalogue (Series Bible Part I, Part V); the oath to record and never intervene (Vol I §5.3; Vol VI §0.1 table); the three rules of the Veil, quoted exactly (Book One Ch14 epigraph, 'Precept of the Silent Veil', manuscript l.4167, l.4223); the House in the deep Woods for eleven hundred years, its motto 'What is written is not lost' over the arch in pitched notation, 'Mausoleum of Chords' as the Synod's survey name (Vol V §3); desks cleaned with vinegar on the last day of every month (Book One Ch14, l.4135); 'Sable' as a Veil designation, not a name (Series Bible Part VIII); 'the voice for entries' (Vol V §3); 'retained against need' as Office doctrine (Vol VI §3.5). The scribe's sealed name 'kept against the day' is written to sit under the Office's later cabinet of staff cores, 'Against the day' (Vol VI §3.3), without saying so; the Office's use of names is not stated. [PROPOSED]: the Rule as a written book and all its text beyond the three rules; the Prior; the scribe's name sealed in a cabinet and returned at the door; the Memoryday reading (follows Vol VI §0.1 The Rota, itself [PROPOSED]); Umber, copyist; the surveyors' visit c. 290 SR; the Office's receiving stamp. Library: the Veil's scriptorium in the Mausoleum.

title: The Honest Fire: A Sermon Between the Beats
author: Furnace-Priest Kell
origin: Cinderhold; printed by subscription of the Deep Guilds
summary: A Cinderhold priest's forge-lighting sermon arguing that heat is the only honest law in the world, because it alone admits what it consumes.
text: THE HONEST FIRE. Preached by the Furnace-Priest Kell at the forge-lighting of the Hearth Feast, in Stillmonth of 418, on the lower tiers, and taken down by a Guild clerk who set a stroke wherever the Great Beat fell, as those who heard it will remember. The Basilica has declared it unsound. It is printed by subscription of the Deep Guilds, who have declared the Basilica cold.

Still standing? | Good. | Then listen between the strokes, | because I will not shout over them. | Nobody shouts over the Beat. | That is the first thing Cinderhold teaches | and the last thing the Church will learn.
(The clerk set the strokes for the first page only. After that, he says, any Cinderholder will hear them for himself, and nobody else deserves to.)

I am a priest of the Pure Note. I hold it. I have held it at the forge-lighting for thirty years. I am not here tonight to tell you the one note is false. I am here to tell you that of the eight laws of the world, only one has ever told us the truth about itself, and it is ours.

Consider the others, as the Church teaches them. Growth gives: the apple, the wheat, the oak. Light gives the day. Mass gives the floor under you and the weight of your child in your arms. Time gives your years, Velocity your winds, Memory your dead, kept. Gift, gift, gift, says the Church, and the glass in the ground the greatest gift of all, the Light's surplus, given for nothing to be burned for nothing. Eight laws, eight presents, and never once a bill.
I have kept a furnace since I was nine years old. I tell you I have never been given anything for nothing in my life, and neither has the world.

Heat does not pretend. Heat says: give me the coal and I will give you warmth, and the coal is gone. Give me the ore and I will give you iron, and the mountain is less by that much. Fire eats, and says it eats, and leaves you ash for a receipt. That is why I call it holy. Not because it is kind. It is not kind. Every one of you has buried someone it took. It is holy because it is the only law in the world that has never once told a man it loved him.

Now. The Church says the glass is surplus. I have a question for the Church, and I put it at the forge-lighting because this is the one night in the year they cannot stop me. Go down to Tier Eleven, where the Guild men cut the richest seams on the continent, and lay your ear against the face the way they do at the end of a shift, when they think nobody is watching. Then come back up and tell me that surplus whispers.

I do not know what the glass was before it was glass. I am a furnace-priest; I know nothing I have not burned. But I know that everything that burns was something first. The coal was a forest. The tallow was a beast. Nothing on this earth comes to the fire without having been something else, and a man who burns a thing and will not ask what it was is not grateful. He is only comfortable.

And the Cold Burn. Our fires freeze in the grate, and our frost scalds, and the ember-blind walk the lower tiers with nothing left alight in them, and the Church calls it a sickness of the flat world and sends us a hymn. I will tell you what I think it is. I think we have drawn on Heat since my grandfather's day as if it were a gift, and it has begun at last to behave like one. A gift is cold. A gift costs the giver everything and the getter nothing, and it comes with no receipt; and that is the fire we have now, fire that takes nothing and gives nothing and lies in the grate looking like fire. We taught it that. We taught it to lie.

So here is my heresy, and you may carry it out of the gate tonight. Every honest thing consumes, and says so: the forge, the furnace, a worker's back, a mother's sleep. If a man tells you he gives and takes nothing, he is a god or a liar, and I have never yet met a god. If a law of the world tells you the same, ask it what it is eating.

The Basilica writes that I have made an idol of a furnace. The Basilica has never stood at one. I invite it. Let a Flambeau come down to the lower tiers and hold the Pure Note in front of the Great Beat for one shift, and keep his hand on it, and then we will talk about idols.

Now light the forges. On the ingot, light them. And when the first heat comes up off the coal into your faces, do not thank it. It does not want thanks. Pay it. Give it what it asks, and look at what it leaves, and remember the price; because the day you stop remembering what the fire costs is the day you will believe anything anybody tells you is free.
Still standing? | Then keep your hand on it.
notes: Canon: Furnace-Priest Kell, fifties, the heretic who holds that heat is the only honest Anchor because it consumes and admits to consuming (Vol II Realm III; Ignatius's interest in him is left out so as not to invent facts about Ignatius); Kell is also one of the Eleven Houses (Vol II); Cinderhold speaking between the hammer-falls of the Great Beat, the four-beat pulse (brief; Vol II Realm III); 'Still standing', 'On the ingot', 'cold' meaning cowardly, 'he kept his hand on it' as the highest praise (Vol II dialect); Tier Eleven and the eleven tiers (Vol II); the Deep Guilds mine the richest glass seams and know the deep glass whispers (Series Bible Part VI, Part VII); the Cold Burn, fire that freezes and frost that scalds, the ember-blind (Part VI, Part IV law-rot); the Church's teaching that glass is the Light's generous surplus (Part III); the Hearth Feast, the forge-lighting on the first Hearthday of Stillmonth, Cinderhold's guild rite (Vol VII §4); siphoning as an industry since 372 (Part V), hence 'since my grandfather's day'. Kell only suspects what glass is; nothing is stated. [PROPOSED]: this sermon, its printing by the Deep Guilds, the Basilica's judgement of it, the clerk's beat-strokes, Kell as a priest of the Pure Note who has held it thirty years. Library: brought to the Oakhaven quarry by a Cinderhold bore-man; could also be found in the Bonded Store at Stillwater.

title: The Oakhaven Works: A Prospectus to Subscribers
author: the Consortium of Bores, by order of the Seven Chairs (Lorimer Stannard, Secretary to the Subscription)
origin: the Consortium's counting-house, Brass Quarter, the Organum
summary: The Consortium's invitation to invest in the new works at Oakhaven, generous with confidence and sparing with figures.
text: THE CONSORTIUM OF BORES. The Oakhaven Works, in the Resonant Reach. A Prospectus for the Second Subscription, issued by order of the Seven Chairs and approved under the hand of the First.
To the subscriber. The Consortium has the honour to invite your part in what the Chairs do not hesitate to call the most promising undertaking of the age.

THE SEAM. The Oakhaven Root lies beneath the old quarry of that town. Our surveyors, who are not given to poetry, describe it as the most generous resonant body yet found on the continent. It is alive in the agricultural sense: it grows, it renews itself, it gives. Where a seam of stone is spent, a living seam refreshes. We do not expect the subscriber to take this on trust, and so we have not burdened this prospectus with figures, which in the case of a seam of this character could only understate it.

THE METHOD. The works are sunk by the Vance Sequence, the Consortium's own method, used on every great bore since 409 and lately much improved by the finest mathematical minds in the Organum. Revision follows revision. The subscriber may rest assured that the Root will be approached with all the care that the most advanced resonant engineering of the age can bring to it.

THE TOWN. Oakhaven is a loyal and grateful town. It was the Consortium's grain, forty wagons of it, that brought the Reach through the famine after the Screaming Year, and the Reach has not forgotten. The Governor is a man of sense. The labour is local, willing, strong in the arm and used to hard country. It is paid in Consortium scrip, redeemable at the works store, which keeps the subscriber's money in the subscriber's own house.
Supplementary labour for the pumps is supplied under contract by the Office of the Catalogue. It asks no wage, no lodging and no rest, and gives no trouble of any kind.
SECURITY. The works enjoy the protection of a detachment of the Carillon Legions. Replacement components for the garrison are delivered by air on a regular schedule, at no charge to the subscription.

OF THE SO-CALLED RISKS. The subscriber may have read, in the less responsible papers of the Rust Coast, that the Reach is 'going soft'. We answer that the Reach has always been soft. It is orchard country. Indeed the vigour of the seam already shows itself, most agreeably, in the town above it. Saplings come up between the cobbles in a night. Hair and nails grow at a rate the townsfolk find remarkable, and the barbers of Oakhaven have never been busier. A local complaint called burl-sickness, long known in the province and wholly unconnected with the works, is attended by the Synod's Surgeon-Grafters, to whose good work the Consortium contributes generously.

It has been put about that the hounds are bolder in the Reach of late. The Consortium keeps no hounds and cannot speak for them. The town has in hand a scheme of hedging, of approved local design, which will make Oakhaven the quietest town in the Reach and, the Chairs believe, the most productive.

It has also been asked whether the Church takes an interest in the works. The Church takes an interest in everything, and the Consortium welcomes it. Where the Church and the Consortium are at one, nothing in the province can stand against them, and they are at one on every point that touches a subscriber.

RETURNS. A dividend will be declared on the Dial Day following the casing, payable in sovereigns at the Organum or, at the subscriber's choice, in scrip at the works. The Chairs do not think it proper to name a figure. They will say only that no subscriber to the Consortium's great works at the Dawning Spire has ever once been asked to return a dividend.

HOW TO SUBSCRIBE. Shares of ten sovereigns, in lots of ten, are received at the Consortium's counting-house in the Brass Quarter, or by the Resident Factor at the Oakhaven works, whose receipt is stamped with the drill-and-wheel. Subscriptions close when the bore reaches the casing. The Chairs anticipate that this will be soon.

The Seven Chairs commend the Oakhaven Works to you in the confident expectation that it will repay everything that is put into it. What the ground gives, the Consortium gathers. The Root is generous. It has never yet refused anyone anything.
Lorimer Stannard, Secretary to the Subscription. Firstfruit, 417.
notes: Canon: the Consortium of Bores, seven chairs, the First held by Ysolde Carrow (not named here) (Series Bible Part VII); the Oakhaven quarry bore begun in 417 (Part V); the Consortium's grain, 'forty wagons of grain and a paper', after the Cascade famine (Book One Ch2, manuscript l.840-850); the Vance Sequence used on every major bore since 409, revised in an Arbiterium hand (Book One Ch2, l.722-740); Consortium scrip, green and black, the drill-and-wheel stamp, the Resident Factor (Book One Ch2, Ch4; brief); Hollows working the quarry pumps (Book One Ch5, Part XI) and crates of replacement cores for the garrison delivered by air (Ch4, Ch8), both told only in the Consortium's euphemism; the law going soft: saplings splitting cobbles, fingernails growing overnight, the burl-sick and the Synod's Grafters (Part VI, the Reach); the Hedge planted in autumn 417 (Phase 20-21 Rulings); the Brass Quarter of the Organum (Book One Ch2); Dial Day (Vol VII §4); Rust Coast papers (Vol II). The Rite, Stage Nine and the bore's purpose are not mentioned. [PROPOSED]: the Second Subscription and this prospectus; Lorimer Stannard; share price and lots; the motto 'What the ground gives, the Consortium gathers'; the hedging scheme described as already in hand by Firstfruit 417 (moved from Reedmonth in review: the Hedge was proposed only after the hounds came in high summer 417, lib_a_wool_wall). Library: the Greenhall, among the Governor's or Factor's papers.
